cf.title: Fix PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc overflow when a year does not fit "yyyy"

input.subject: Fix PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc overflow when a year does not fit "yyyy"

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a or 1b: the overflow is reproducible with ASan and the goal is a bug fix. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is a fixable level 2 point: the patch targets stable branches but does not state the return value or the contents of outbuf on the new failure. A committer who knows ECPG must decide between an error and wider output, and how far back the fix goes.

brief.title: Fix PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc buffer overflow for years above 9999
brief.problem: PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() writes a year of five or more digits over the four-character "yyyy" token, so a caller who sizes outbuf as strlen(fmtstring)+1 gets a heap buffer overflow. This affects ECPG programs that format dates with year >= 10000.
brief.proposed_design: When a replacement is longer than its token, PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() rejects it and sets errno to PGTYPES_DATE_BAD_DATE. The patch adds a dt_test case that formats 10000-01-01 with "yyyy".
user_visible_surface: PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() now fails with errno PGTYPES_DATE_BAD_DATE for years that do not fit the "yyyy" token, where before it wrote past the token.
author_claims: ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow on the next strstr() in the token loop.
Callers usually size outbuf as strlen(fmtstring)+1, as dt_test does.
The fix belongs in stable branches (CommitFest target version: stable).
brief.thread_state: Zsolt Parragi found a wrong line number in the expected stderr, and v2 fixed it. David Rowley asked the author to stop sending reminders, and no one has reviewed the design.
unclear: The material does not say whether other tokens, such as month or day names, can also produce a longer replacement.
The patch does not say what the function returns on failure, or what outbuf holds.
The material does not say whether any documentation lists the new failure case.
The thread does not discuss whether turning a five-digit year into an error breaks existing callers that use larger buffers.
The material does not say how far back the fix should go.
search_queries: pgtypeslib fix out of bounds write

objections.title: Back-branch change to the PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() failure contract is not defined
objections.failure_scenario: An ECPG application on a minor release formats far-future dates with a trailing "yyyy" into a large buffer, then prints outbuf without checking the return value. After the upgrade the call fails, and outbuf holds whatever the patch leaves there. The user finds out from wrong report output, not from an error.
objections.argument: The patch targets stable branches and turns a case that had no error into a new error, with errno set to PGTYPES_DATE_BAD_DATE. The commit message does not say what the function returns or what outbuf holds on this failure, and no documentation hunk lists the case. For a library contract changed in a minor release, a committer would likely ask for both to be stated. A committer would also likely ask whether a caller with a large enough buffer ever got a correct five-digit year before the patch.
objections.author_must_show: What do the return value and outbuf look like on the new failure, and did any caller with a large buffer get correct output before the patch?

critic.reasoning: The commit message and thread do not say what PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() returns or what outbuf holds on the new failure. A caller with a zero-filled larger buffer and a trailing "yyyy" could get a correct five-digit year today, so the back-branch behavior change needs an answer.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() in libpgtypes gains a new failure case for callers; the signature does not change.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch closes a client-side heap buffer overflow in libpgtypes.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CommitFest entry targets stable branches, and the fix turns a case with no error into an error.

doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What does PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() return, and what does outbuf hold, when the year does not fit "yyyy"?
Did a caller with a buffer larger than strlen(fmtstring)+1 get a correct five-digit year before the patch, and does that caller now get an error?
Can any other token, such as a month or day name, produce a replacement longer than the token, and does the length check cover it?
Which stable branches should receive the fix?
Does the ECPG documentation for PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() need to list the new failure case?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows ECPG and pgtypeslib, and who can judge a behavior change in a client library on stable branches. No such committer has reviewed the design in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new error return in a shipped client library on every stable branch that gets the fix, and for any ECPG application that relied on the old output.
committability.author_follow_up: The author sent v2 after the report in message #3 about the wrong line number in the expected stderr, which suggests the author stays for fixes.

priority.reason: The patch is about 6 KiB, touches one pgtypeslib file plus dt_test, and fixes an out-of-bounds write that only ECPG programs with years of 10000 or more reach. It waits on a committer who knows ECPG to settle the failure contract and the back-patch range.

provisional_note: Without the code, the return value and the state of outbuf on failure could not be checked. Whether the length check covers every token, including negative years printed with "%04u", is also unverified.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Show subtransaction overflow status
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch exposes each backend's subtransaction count and whether its subtransaction cache has overflowed, so DBAs can find the sessions that force SLRU lookups for all concurrent queries. It started as two new pg_stat_activity columns and was reworked into a single function returning a record per backend.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that effort should go into fixing the subtransaction overflow performance problem itself, because monitoring does not relieve the problem and could cause compatibility problems once a fundamental fix changes how this area works. Andres Freund agreed and asked for the entry to be marked rejected, also noting it had been failing on cfbot for weeks. The author agreed that a real fix would make the status reporting pointless and marked it rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If the subxact overflow business is causing
real-world performance problems, let's find a way to fix that, not put
effort into monitoring tools that do little to actually alleviate anyone's
pain.

precedents_retrieved.title: Nonreplayable XLog records by means of overflows and >MaxAllocSize lengths
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds checks in xloginsert.c so that the WAL insertion API cannot assemble a record larger than xlogreader can read (MaxAllocSize, later a fixed 1020 MiB limit), and cannot overflow xl_tot_len through repeated XLogRegisterData() calls. It also documents the record size limit in the XLogRecord spec.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier committed part of the patch, the API changes and the uint16 block data checks. He then asked for a rebase of the rest, and the author did not reply for two commitfests, so the entry was returned with feedback. After it was closed, Andres Freund noted that the new record-too-large ERROR usually happens inside a critical section and so becomes a PANIC. He suggested building large records such as the commit record before the critical section.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
No replies after 4 weeks, so I have marked this entry as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: ECPG: Declare Statement
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add DECLARE STATEMENT support to ECPG, so that an AT clause given once binds a statement name to a connection. Later PREPARE, EXECUTE, DECLARE CURSOR and similar statements then use that connection without repeating AT, with ecpglib functions such as ECPGdo changed to look up the connection by statement name.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. They end in November 2016 with Michael Meskes waiting for a patch after the design was clarified, and the entry was returned with feedback in November 2017.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve overflow checks potentially optimized away by compiler
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal rewrites signed-integer overflow checks such as x + y < x into precondition tests such as x > INT_MAX - y, so compilers that treat signed overflow as undefined (icc, pathcc, clang) cannot remove them. Later versions extended this to int.c, int8.c and btree_gist, added INT16 overflow macros and added regression tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the final version, so Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback. Earlier, Greg Stark wrote that he was coming around to Tom's view that the change was a lot of hassle for little gain. Tom's own message giving that view is not among the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And nobody got interested into that, marking as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add generate_series(date,date,[step])
precedents_retrieved.objectors: David Steele, Tom Lane, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds generate_series(date, date) and generate_series(date, date, integer), which return dates with a step in days. It returns an empty set when either endpoint is infinite.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Adding generate_series(date, date, integer) changes how the parser resolves existing calls such as generate_series('01-01-2000'::date, '01-04-2000'::date, '7 days'). Those calls now pick the integer step and fail, where before they resolved to the timestamptz version. A rename to generate_dates() removed the main benefit for supporters, and David Steele and Tom Lane moved to -1. The author withdrew the patch, and Robert Haas judged a generate_series(date, date, interval) variant too different to redesign that late in the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So if you had written such a call with an interval literal and didn't bother to cast the literal, your code would break.

precedents_retrieved.title: Correct negative/zero year in to_date/to_timestamp
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes to_date and to_timestamp so that a negative year in the input (YYYY) maps to the same BC year, instead of one year earlier, and year 0 raises an error. It also makes a negative year or century override the era indicator.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas and Tom Lane held that input such as '-2-06-01' does not match the format 'YYYY-MM-DD', so its current result is an implementation artifact that should not be redefined. Tom Lane added that the patch adds an error for year zero while still accepting other bad input, and that changes at the margins create another backward-compatibility hazard for a later rewrite of to_date. Both voted to reject, and the author accepted that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I'm not seeing the argument that hacking at the margins
like this moves us forward on either point; what it does do is create
another backward-compatibility hazard for any such rewrite.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character...
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert COPY OUT to follow the pre-8.3 handling of ASCII control characters, namely that \r, \n, \t, \b, \f, \v are dumped as those two-character representations rather than a backslash and the literal control character. I had made it do the other to save some code, but this was ill-advised, because dump files in which these characters appear literally are prone to newline mangling.  Fortunately, doing it the old way should only cost a few more lines of code, and not slow down the copy loop materially. Per bug #3795 from Lou Duchez.

precedents_retrieved.title: Refactor ECPGconnect() and allow IPv6 connection
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch refactors ECPGconnect() so that ECPG connection strings accept bracketed IPv6 host addresses such as 'tcp:postgresql://[::1]/postgres', in the same way as libpq. It adds new parse functions in ECPG that copy libpq's URI parsing, including a rewrite of parse_options().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the patch copies libpq's URI parsing logic into ECPG and asked for a consolidated approach. The author agreed and planned to rework the patch so that ECPG passes the string to PQconnectdb() and skips its own parsing. No new patch followed, and David G. Johnston moved the entry to "Waiting on Author" in August 2021.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As you are writing in your first bullet point and as mentioned
upthread, it does not strike me as a great idea to have a duplicate
logic doing the parsing of URIs, even if libpq accepts multiple
hosts/ports as an option.  Couldn't we have a better consolidation
here?

precedents_retrieved.title: Support UTF16/32 host variable in ECPG
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add Oracle Pro*C compatible Unicode host variable types to ECPG, a utext type and a variable-length UVARCHAR type, holding UTF-16 or UTF-32 data. ECPG would convert between these variables and the database character set (at first only UTF8), with an environment variable to select endianness.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback after a high-level review. It no longer applied, had whitespace errors and no documentation, and added four undocumented libpq functions without saying why client_encoding was not enough. He also found the patch too large to review as one piece: about 800 lines of code and 20k lines of tests, which he asked to split into smaller steps. He was unsure the feature was useful, and without documentation he could not judge it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With a high-level look, this patch requires a bit more work.. I am
unsure as well if that's a feature which would prove to be useful, but
without documentation it is hard to make an opinion of it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert my bad decision of about a year ago to make PortalDefineQuery responsible for copying the query string into the new Portal.  Such copying is unnecessary in the common code path through exec_simple_query, and in this case it can be enormously expensive because the string might contain a large number of individual commands; we were copying the entire, long string for each command, resulting in O(N^2) behavior for N commands. (This is the cause of bug #4079.)  A second problem with it is that PortalDefineQuery really can't risk error, because if it elog's before having set up the Portal, we will leak the plancache refcount that the caller is trying to hand off to the portal.  So go back to the design in which the caller is responsible for making sure everything is copied into the portal if necessary.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
Reverted commit(s): Track more precisely query locations for nested statements; Fix regression with location calculation of nested statements; pg_stat_statements: Add tests for nested queries with level tracking
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the two following commits:
- 499edb09741b, track more precisely query locations for nested
statements.
- 06450c7b8c70, a follow-up fix of 499edb09741b with query locations.
The test introduced in this commit is not reverted.  This is proving
useful to track a problem that only pgaudit was able to detect.

These prove to have issues with the tracking of SELECT statements, when
these use multiple parenthesis which is something supported by the
grammar.  Incorrect location and lengths are causing pg_stat_statements
to become confused, failing its job in query normalization with
potential out-of-bound writes because the location and the length may
not match with what can be handled.  A lot of the query patterns
discussed when this issue was reported have no test coverage in the main
regression test suite, or the recovery test 027_stream_regress.pl would
have caught the problems as pg_stat_statements is loaded by the node
running the regression tests.  A first step would be to improve the test
coverage to stress more the query normalization logic.

A different portion of this work was done in 45e0ba30fc40, with the
addition of tests for nested queries.  These can be left in the tree.
They are useful to track the way inner queries are currently tracked by
PGSS with non-top-level entries, and will be useful when reconsidering
in the future the work reverted here.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. The precedent search returned no rows on the same or a similar idea, and no thread message points to an earlier discussion of this overflow or of PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc, so the prior-attempts angle has nothing to raise.
The other compatibility points look sound. The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog entry or dump object, and it reuses an existing errno value.

The patch changes only the formatting logic of PGTYPESdate_fmt_asc() in the client-side libpgtypes and its regression test. It adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, wire protocol or replication state, and it changes no function signature or exported struct, so the library ABI and backpatching are unaffected from this angle. The new error return in stable branches is a behaviour change for callers, which other angles cover.

The patch closes a client-side heap overflow in libpgtypes and adds no new privilege, default, or exposure, so I found no security objection. Without the code I cannot confirm that the length check covers every token, including negative years printed with %04u.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to object to: a bounded fix to an out-of-bounds write in pgtypeslib adds no API, hook or work for code that does not use it. Two points remain open: no ecpg committer has reviewed it, and the new error in stable branches affects callers that gave a larger outbuf and got "10000" back.

This is a bug fix for an out-of-bounds write in an existing ECPG library function. No existing feature, option or extension gives callers a safe result here, so the need is not already met. Choices such as error versus wider output, and the back-patch scope, belong to other angles.

This is a fix for a heap buffer overflow in a shipped libpq-adjacent library, so demand is not the right test. Years of 10000 or more are rare, but an out-of-bounds write that ASan reproduces (message #1) needs fixing whether or not many callers hit it.
